mainEntity.name: Can I be allergic to acrylic dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: True allergic reactions to fully cured dental-grade acrylic are uncommon but not impossible. A small number of people may have sensitivity to residual monomer components within the acrylic. Symptoms may include persistent redness, soreness, or swelling of the gum tissue beneath the denture. If you experience these symptoms, it is important to arrange a dental review. There may be several possible explanations for oral discomfort, including poor fit or fungal infection, and a clinical examination is needed to identify the cause and discuss appropriate options.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my acrylic dentures no longer fit properly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Signs that dentures may no longer fit well include movement during speaking or eating, soreness or sore patches on the gums, difficulty chewing, or a noticeable change in facial appearance. Oral anatomy naturally changes over time as the underlying bone remodels after tooth loss, which can alter how dentures sit. If you notice any of these changes, a dental review is advisable. Your dentist can assess the fit and discuss options such as relining, rebasing, or fabricating a new set of dentures if appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to sleep in acrylic dentures?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental professionals advise removing dentures overnight. This allows the gum tissue beneath the denture base to rest, recover, and receive normal saliva flow, which helps maintain tissue health. Sleeping in dentures consistently has been associated with an increased risk of denture stomatitis — a fungal infection of the soft tissues. There may be certain clinical situations where a dentist recommends wearing dentures overnight, but this should be discussed individually during a clinical appointment rather than based on general preference.

mainEntity.name: How often should acrylic dentures be professionally checked?

acceptedAnswer.text: As a general guide, denture wearers benefit from professional dental reviews at least once a year, though your dentist may recommend more frequent appointments depending on your individual circumstances. These reviews allow your dental team to assess the fit and condition of the denture, examine your oral tissues for any changes, and provide cleaning advice. Skipping routine reviews can mean that changes in fit or early oral health concerns go unaddressed for longer than necessary.

mainEntity.name: Are there alternatives to acrylic dentures that might be more suitable?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, there are alternative denture materials, including Valplast dentures and cobalt-chrome partial denture frameworks. Each has distinct clinical advantages and limitations. Flexible dentures may suit patients who want a metal-free, aesthetically discreet partial denture, whilst cobalt-chrome frameworks offer greater strength and a thinner profile. The most appropriate material for any individual depends on factors including the number and location of missing teeth, bite forces, bone structure, and personal preferences. A dentist or clinical dental technician can discuss these options during a consultation and help identify the most suitable approach for your specific needs.

mainEntity.name: Can acrylic dentures be repaired if they crack or break?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in many cases acrylic dentures can be repaired by a dental laboratory, particularly for straightforward cracks or fractures. It is important not to attempt home repairs using general-purpose adhesives, as these can be unsafe and may distort the denture's fit, potentially causing harm to oral tissues. If your denture is damaged, contact your dental practice as soon as possible. Your dentist or clinical dental technician can assess whether repair is appropriate or whether replacement may be a more suitable long-term solution.
